teaser: The Louvre's biggest painting hangs right behind the backs of the Mona Lisa crowd.
review_notes:
Dimensions 6.77 x 9.94 m, usually called the largest painting in the Louvre; about 130 figures (standard count).
Contract of June 1562 with the Benedictines of San Giorgio Maggiore: 324 ducats, meals and a barrel of wine, finest pigments required; finished in about 15 months (autumn 1563).
Refectory designed by Palladio.
Musicians as portraits of Veronese (white, viola da gamba), Titian (red, bass instrument), Tintoretto and Bassano: an old tradition first written down long after Veronese's death, not documented.
Hourglass on the musicians' table: reported in the literature, only a tiny shape in our image; the spot covers the whole table.
Butchers carving meat directly above Christ, read as lamb and as a hint of sacrifice: common interpretation.
1797: canvas cut in two by French troops for transport, sewn back in Paris. 1815: Louvre kept it as too fragile and sent Le Brun's Feast in the House of Simon to Venice instead.
1992 restoration accidents (water leak, then fall of the canvas with five tears, no figures damaged): check details.
1573 Inquisition hearing concerned another feast painting (now called The Feast in the House of Levi); Veronese's answer is paraphrased.
2007 full-size facsimile by Factum Arte installed in the refectory of San Giorgio Maggiore.
Cat at lower right (x 0.875, y 0.965) is small: check the find spot in the app.

lesson.text: Almost ten meters wide and nearly seven tall (about 32 by 22 feet). That is the floor area of a small apartment, hung on a wall. The Wedding at Cana is the largest painting in the Louvre, and every day thousands of people stand in front of it with their backs turned. They are looking at the Mona Lisa, on the opposite wall.

It was never meant for a museum. In 1562 the Benedictine monks of San Giorgio Maggiore, on an island facing Venice, ordered it for the end wall of their refectory, the hall where they ate. Paolo Veronese, then 34, had to fill the whole wall, as if the room opened onto a second, far noisier dining room.
The contract survives. Veronese was promised 324 ducats, his meals for as long as the job lasted, and a barrel of wine. A fitting bonus for this subject. He delivered about fifteen months later.

The subject comes from the Gospel of John. Jesus and his mother are guests at a wedding in the village of Cana. The wine runs out. Jesus has the servants fill stone jars with water, and when it is poured, it is wine: his first miracle. So where, in this crowd of about 130 people, does the miracle happen?

lesson.title: Looking for the miracle
lesson.text: Four stops. The order may surprise you.

spots.title: The still center
spots.text: Jesus sits exactly in the middle, with a faint halo, and looks straight out at you. He is the only guest who does nothing: no eating, no talking, no gesture.

spots.title: Water, now wine
spots.text: A barefoot servant in yellow tips a heavy stone jar. What runs into the golden jug is red. The miracle is a kitchen task, done down in the right foreground.

spots.title: The taster
spots.text: The man in the white and green brocade lifts his glass and studies it. He is the master of the feast, and he is working out why the best wine has come last.

spots.title: The newlyweds
spots.text: The bride and groom sit at the far left end of the table, dressed like Venetian royalty, being handed a glass. At their own wedding they have been pushed into a corner.

lesson.text: A miracle that happens at the edges, a couple squeezed into the corner, and a Christ who sits motionless in the noise. Veronese has moved a village wedding from ancient Galilee to the richest party Venice could imagine in 1563: silk, turbans, silver plates, marble columns.
Veronese paints a Bible story as a Venetian banquet. The sacred event is there, quiet and central, and you have to find it inside the party.
A hundred and thirty guests could easily turn into mush. They do not, because under the fuss lies a plan as firm as the architecture of the hall it was painted for. Three lines are enough to show it.

lines.label: The table
lines.text: The table bends like a U, open toward us. The empty side is ours: the monks eating in the hall below completed the circle.

lines.label: The balustrade
lines.text: A stone railing cuts the picture in two. Below: people, cloth, food, crowded and warm. Above: cool sky and white stone, with far fewer figures.

lines.label: The axis
lines.text: One vertical runs through Christ and rises into the open sky. Left and right halves balance around it like two wings of a building.

lesson.text: Follow that axis upward from Christ's head. On the terrace right above him, servants are cutting up meat, often said to be lamb. For a Christian viewer, the lamb means sacrifice: over the first miracle hangs a hint of the death to come. A party picture with a shadow in the middle.

Venetians long loved to say that the musicians in the center are portraits. The one in white with the viola would be Veronese himself, and the old man in red with the big bass instrument would be Titian, the grand master of Venetian painting. Nothing proves it, but nobody has wanted to give the story up.

Veronese also filled his feast with things the Gospel never mentions: jesters, dogs, servants on the roofs. He clearly enjoyed it. One animal is so absorbed in its own business that it ignores the miracle happening a step away.
A cat is playing somewhere at this wedding. Can you catch it?

spots.title: The cat
spots.text: Rolled on its back in the bottom right corner, it claws at a carved face on the big stone jar. One of the jars of the miracle has become a cat toy.

lesson.text: This taste for extras caught up with him. Ten years later, another of his giant feasts brought him before the Inquisition, the Church court, which asked what clowns, drunks and dogs were doing at a holy supper. His answer, in short: painters take the same liberties as poets and madmen.

The monks had asked for the best colors money could buy, and Venice, a trading port, was the place to get them. The blues come from lapis lazuli, a stone carried from Afghanistan and ground to powder. Veronese sets them against oranges, greens and pinks so that each color makes its neighbor ring louder.

spots.title: The quartet
spots.text: Four musicians play right under Christ. A small hourglass is said to stand on their table: a reminder that music, like the party, runs out.

spots.title: Mary
spots.text: In a dark veil at her son's right hand, the only somber figure at the table. In the Gospel she is the one who notices that the wine is gone.

spots.title: The carvers
spots.text: On the terrace above Christ, men bend over a table cutting up meat for the next course.

spots.title: Two hounds
spots.text: Two pale hunting dogs tied on one leash. One stands alert, the other lies chewing at something on the floor.

spots.title: The bell tower
spots.text: A white tower against the sky, in the style of the newest Venetian buildings. Cana has become a dream version of the city.

spots.title: Gatecrashers
spots.text: Onlookers lean over the ledges and cling to the cornice to watch the feast from above.

spots.title: The plates
spots.text: Behind the columns, shelves of gleaming dishes, and servants carrying more down the stairs. Showing off your tableware was part of a Venetian banquet.

lesson.text: For more than two centuries the monks ate under it. Then, in 1797, Napoleon's army took Venice and went shopping. The canvas was too big to move, so the soldiers cut it in two, rolled the halves and shipped them to Paris, where it was sewn back together. When France returned looted art in 1815, the Louvre called this one too fragile to travel and sent another painting to Venice instead.

The painting's worst day came in a museum. In 1992, during a restoration in the Louvre, the huge canvas fell while it was being lifted, and its metal support tore several holes in it. By luck the tears missed the figures, and they were mended.
Next time you see a photo of the crowd around the Mona Lisa, check the wall behind the phones. A wedding with 130 guests, two hounds and a cat is going on there, and almost nobody has turned around.

The monks' wall in Venice is no longer bare. In 2007 a full-size copy, made from high-resolution scans of the original and printed with every crack and brushstroke, was installed in the refectory of San Giorgio Maggiore, at the exact spot Veronese painted for.

quiz.question: For which kind of room was the painting made?
options: The dining hall of a monastery
quiz.explanation: The monks of San Giorgio Maggiore ordered it for their refectory, where they ate.

quiz.question: Where does the water turned into wine actually appear?
options: In the right foreground, where a servant pours from a stone jar
On the terrace above the table
quiz.explanation: A servant in yellow pours red wine from a jar into a golden jug at the lower right.

quiz.question: Where do the bride and groom sit?
options: Next to Christ in the center
At the far left end of the table
quiz.explanation: Veronese pushes the couple to the left corner and gives the center to Christ.

quiz.question: How did the canvas leave Venice in 1797?
options: It was sold by the monks
Napoleon's soldiers cut it in two and shipped it to Paris
It was given to the French king as a gift
quiz.explanation: French troops cut it in half, rolled it and sent it to Paris.

quiz.question: What separates the crowded lower half from the airy upper half?
quiz.explanation: The railing divides the banquet below from the sky and architecture above.

facts.text: Veronese's contract included a barrel of wine.
facts.explanation: He was promised 324 ducats, his meals and a barrel of wine.

facts.text: The painting went back to Venice in 1815 with the rest of Napoleon's loot.
facts.explanation: The Louvre kept it as too fragile to travel and sent another painting instead.

facts.text: Historical documents prove that the musician in red is Titian.
facts.explanation: It is an old tradition that nothing proves.
